overview: Lübeck remained a small trading republic long after the medieval Hanse’s greatest days. This card follows the eighteenth- and nineteenth-century city, through French occupation, constitutional reform and German unification. The imported 1715 to 1878 dates are only map coverage. Its 1715 outline is grossly overbroad and must not be read as territory actually ruled by Lübeck.

periods.title: An old city republic
periods.summary: Lübeck maintained its own civic government and trading institutions.

periods.title: War and French occupation
periods.summary: French occupation interrupted the city’s autonomy.

periods.title: Restoration and a changing city
periods.summary: Lübeck joined the German Confederation in 1815 and the German Empire in 1871.

sections.title: A small state in a changing Germany

items.text: War reached the streets on 6 November 1806, when French troops fought Prussian forces led by Blücher at Lübeck. The French entered and plundered the city. Occupation continued until 1813, so the free-city label on a long timeline should not suggest uninterrupted independence.

In 1820, Hamburg, Bremen, Frankfurt and Lübeck chose Lübeck as the home of their shared appeals court. These four surviving free cities cooperated on justice while keeping separate governments. A small state could supply an important institution to its neighbors.

The upheavals of 1848 brought an elected parliament and opened civic citizenship to Jews. Civic citizens could participate, but citizenship and simply living in the city were different categories. The reform therefore widened political participation without giving every resident a vote.

sections.title: Homes hidden behind the grand streets

items.text: Behind imposing merchants’ houses lay narrow alleys lined with tiny rented homes. These housing patterns had medieval roots and remained part of the later city. Porters, day laborers and craftspeople lived in one- or two-storey huts, often with only one room. A handsome street front could conceal a very crowded neighborhood.

Some alleys provided charitable housing. The von Höveln complex had been intended for poor or elderly people since 1483, but its surviving small houses date from a complete rebuilding in 1792. Giving an old foundation new buildings was one way the eighteenth-century city continued to care for selected residents.

Writing sample: a 1797 property record lists “Im Grünen Gang 4 Wohnsäale”, meaning “Four living quarters in the Green Alley.” This German wording is preserved in a modern archive transcription. Such plain inventories help historians recover rented living spaces that seldom appear in grand portraits or ceremonial histories.

sections.title: Older people, kitchens and household comforts

items.text: The medieval Holy Spirit Hospital continued to house older and needy residents. In the early nineteenth century, wooden compartments were inserted into its great hall, giving residents small individual spaces. These were known locally as Kabäuschen. The institution had 170 places, and the last occupants did not leave these old compartments until 1970.

Care inside the hospital depended partly on property far outside its walls. Its foundation owned villages, farmland and estates, including holdings on the island of Poel. Income and accumulated assets helped pay for upkeep and expansion. The money behind a bed in town might begin with land in the countryside.

The Behnhaus, remodeled around 1800 and occupied by the Behn family from 1823, shows a wealthy household’s arrangements. An office and reception room faced the street, while a kitchen behind the main hall sent food upstairs by a small lift. Dinner could change floors without using the staircase.

Three connected salons occupied the first floor, with guest rooms and servants’ chambers higher up. Today’s green patterned wallpaper in the reception room is a reconstruction based on a surviving historical fragment. Conservators also uncovered layers of paint on the woodwork: even a wall can keep a household diary.

The Wakenitz waterworks began operating in 1867. Steam engines lifted river water, sand filters cleaned it, and pumps sent it into a water tower. The combined machinery and filtration made water supply a city-scale engineering task. It required much more than finding a river and hoping for the best.

Railways changed Lübeck’s links with other ports. The line through Büchen was completed in 1851 after opposition from Denmark, which controlled surrounding territory. A direct railway to Hamburg opened in 1865. Routes and neighboring governments mattered to merchants as much as the goods sitting in their warehouses.

Johann Georg Niederegger took over a confectionery business in 1806 and moved into his own premises on Breite Straße in 1822. The firm’s records connect Lübeck’s famous sweet-making tradition with a particular shop and family business. Marzipan history has room for actual shopkeepers as well as tempting legends.

ending.text: Lübeck continued as a German constituent state beyond the map’s 1878 cutoff. Its statehood ended in 1937 under the Greater Hamburg legislation, when it was incorporated into Prussian Schleswig-Holstein. The city itself continued.
